theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: You are leading a team of four making a bolted bracket with hand tools. What should you do before the tools are issued?
options: Hand out every tool in the store so nobody has to wait
Read the drawing, list the steps and pick tools for each
Let each member choose whichever tools they like best
Start cutting at once and decide on the tools as you go

questions.stem: A repair must be done beside a fuel storage tank, where flammable vapour may be present. Which hand tools are usually chosen, along with a permit and gas testing?
options: Hardened steel tools with a bright chrome finish
Any steel tools, as long as the handles are plastic
Ordinary carbon steel tools kept lightly oiled
Non-sparking tools made of a copper alloy

questions.stem: A team member says that with insulated screwdrivers he can safely work on a live circuit. What is the right reply?
options: No: they are a back-up only; isolate and prove dead first
Yes, as long as the handle is marked for 1000 V use
Yes, as long as he wears dry leather welding gloves
Yes, but only on 110 V circuits, never on 220 V ones

questions.stem: Which tapping drill is used before cutting an M10 × 1.5 thread by hand?

8.5 mm
7.5 mm

questions.stem: A set of three hand taps is used to thread a blind hole (a hole that does not go right through). In which order are they used?

Second, then taper, then plug (bottoming)
Taper, then second, then plug (bottoming)

To check that the thread pitch is correct

questions.stem: Before threading the end of a 12 mm steel rod with a die, what should be done to the rod end?

Heat it to red so the die cuts more easily
Paint it so the start of the thread shows
File or grind a small chamfer on it

questions.stem: How should a click-type torque wrench be stored after use?

Wound back to its lowest setting, in its case
Hung up by its head on the shadow board

It is made to turn clockwise only and will not reverse
Its handle is too short to give enough leverage
It needs a battery that runs flat when undoing nuts

questions.stem: A force of 200 N is applied at the end of a spanner, 300 mm from the centre of the nut. What torque is applied?

questions.stem: Which socket is best for undoing a tight, slightly rusted hexagon nut?
options: A 12-point socket one size larger than the nut
A 12-point socket of the exact size
A 6-point socket of the exact size
Any socket that slips on loosely and easily

Pull it so that the load goes on the moving jaw
Strike it with a hammer to free a stubborn nut

Its jaws cannot open wide enough for nuts
It can only be turned anticlockwise

questions.stem: About what point angle is a cold chisel usually ground to for cutting mild steel?
When a cold chisel is sharpened on a bench grinder, why is it dipped in water often?

To stop it overheating and going soft

questions.stem: Which clamp is quickest for holding two plates tight for tacking, and can be locked and released with one hand?

questions.stem: A team will be sawing and filing for several hours. What helps most to prevent strain injuries to wrists and hands?

questions.stem: Why does a team leader use a shadow board and a tool sign-out sheet?

So that tools can be borrowed without asking anyone

questions.stem: During the morning tool check, you find a spanner with spread (opened-out) jaws. As team leader, what should you do?
options: Remove it, tag it unfit for use and record it
Keep it for use on slightly smaller nuts instead
Squeeze the jaws back together in the bench vice

questions.stem: A flat screwdriver tip has become rounded. What is the right way to deal with it?
options: Hammer the tip flat again on the anvil
Heat the tip to red, then quench it in oil

questions.stem: What is the best way to hold a round bar firmly in a vice while filing a flat on it?
options: Between the flat jaws, tightened as hard as possible
Holding it by hand on the bench beside the vice
In vee-grooved jaws or on a vee block
Gripped in a pair of pliers held in the vice

questions.stem: The thread on a bolt must be identified so that a matching nut can be found. Which hand tool is used?
options: A set of feeler gauges, thinnest blade first
A thread pitch (screw pitch) gauge

A centre gauge held against the thread

options: So that the key cannot bend
So that the screw turns faster
Because the long end is softer
So the long arm gives more leverage

questions.stem: Which tool is used to clean the gas holes in the tip (nozzle) of an oxy-fuel cutting torch?
options: A set of tip cleaners

A stiff steel wire brush

questions.stem: Why does a team leader keep a written record of hand tool checks and repairs?
options: To decide which trainee must pay for each lost tool
To give the Centre's auditors something to read

essays.stem: You are leading a team of four to make a batch of steel brackets using only hand tools: marking out, sawing, filing, tapping holes and bolting. Explain how you would plan the job and organise the team and the tools.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by reading the drawing and job card to find the number of brackets, the material, the sizes, tolerances and threads. Then I break the job into steps: mark out, saw, file to size, deburr, drill and tap, check and assemble. For each step I list the tools needed, such as a scriber, square, hacksaw with an 18 TPI blade, files, taps and a tap wrench, a torque wrench and the measuring tools. I check that each tool is in good condition and that we have spares such as blades. I look at the risks, such as cuts from sharp edges, strain from long sawing and filing, and flying chips, and decide on PPE and controls. I share out the work so each member has a clear task, and I rotate tasks to cut down strain. I brief the team on the plan, the quality checks after each step and the time allowed. During the job I check progress and quality, and at the end I make sure the tools are cleaned, checked and returned, and I report on the job.
markingPoints: Reads the drawing and job card and breaks the job into steps
Lists the right tools for each step and checks their condition and spares
Identifies risks and sets PPE and controls
Shares out and rotates tasks, and briefs the team, including quality checks
Monitors progress, then cleans, checks, returns tools and reports

essays.stem: Explain step by step how to cut an M10 thread by hand in a blind hole in 20 mm steel plate, and how you would check the finished thread.
essays.modelAnswer: First I mark and centre punch the hole position, then drill the tapping hole. For M10 × 1.5 the tapping drill is 8.5 mm, found as 10 minus the 1.5 mm pitch or from a tapping chart. The hole is drilled a little deeper than the thread needed, because the tap cannot cut full thread at the very bottom. I chamfer the top of the hole so the tap starts easily. I clamp the plate firmly, fit the taper tap in a tap wrench of the right size, and start it square, checking with a small square from two sides. I use cutting fluid and turn the tap forward about one turn, then back a quarter to a half turn to break the chip. I take the tap out often to clear chips from the blind hole, because packed chips can snap the tap. Then I follow with the second tap and finish with the plug tap to cut full thread near the bottom. I check the thread with an M10 bolt or a thread plug gauge, and clean out the hole.
markingPoints: Correct tapping drill (8.5 mm), drilled deeper than the thread, with a chamfer
Work clamped and tap started square, checked from two sides
Cutting fluid used; turn forward then back to break the chip
Chips cleared often from the blind hole; taps used in order taper, second, plug
Thread checked with a bolt or thread gauge and the hole cleaned

essays.stem: Explain how you would set up an inspection and control system for your team's hand tools, so that tools are safe and none go missing.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would make a register of every hand tool in the team's kit, with a number marked on each tool, so each one can be traced. I would set up a shadow board or foam-cut drawers, so it is easy to see at a glance which tools are out. Tools are signed out and back in on a sheet, with the name, date and time, so we know who has each one. At the start and end of every job, each tool is checked for faults, such as cracked or loose handles, mushroomed heads, spread jaws, worn screwdriver tips and blunt or chipped edges. I would also arrange a full inspection each month, recorded in the register, and use a coloured tag or mark to show the tool passed that month's check. Any faulty tool is tagged 'Do not use', taken out of the kit and recorded for repair or replacement. Tools are counted at the end of the day, especially when working at height or near machinery, so that a lost tool is found before it causes harm.
markingPoints: A numbered register of all tools
Shadow board or foam drawers, and a sign-out and sign-in sheet
Checks before and after each job, with examples of faults
Regular recorded inspections with a pass mark or tag
Faulty tools tagged and removed; tools counted at the end of the day

essays.stem: Describe how to recondition these hand tools safely: a cold chisel with a mushroomed head and a blunt edge, a rounded flat screwdriver tip, and a hammer with a loose wooden handle.
essays.modelAnswer: For the cold chisel, I first grind the mushroomed head back to a smooth, slight chamfer, so that no loose pieces can fly off when it is struck. Then I grind the cutting edge to the right angle, about 60° for mild steel, with the edge slightly curved. I use the bench grinder with its guards and tool rest correctly set, wear a face shield over safety glasses, and dip the chisel in water often so the edge does not overheat and lose its hardness. For the screwdriver, I grind or file the tip so the faces are flat and parallel and the end is square, again keeping it cool; if the tip is cracked or too short, I replace the screwdriver. For the hammer, I do not just soak the handle in water. I take the head off, fit a new, sound handle of the right size so it fills the eye, and drive in a wedge to spread the top of the handle and lock the head. I record each repair in the tool register before returning the tool.
markingPoints: Chisel head dressed to a smooth chamfer so pieces cannot fly off
Chisel edge ground to the right angle, kept cool to keep its hardness
Safe grinder use: guards, tool rest, face shield
Screwdriver tip ground or filed square and flat, or replaced
Hammer: new handle fitted and wedged; repairs recorded

essays.stem: Compare open-ended spanners, ring spanners, adjustable spanners, 6-point and 12-point sockets and torque wrenches. Say which is best for which job and why.
essays.modelAnswer: An open-ended spanner is quick to fit and can go on a nut from the side, for example on a pipe union, but it grips only two flats, so it can slip and round off a tight nut. A ring spanner grips all six corners, so it is better for breaking a tight nut loose, though it must be lifted off and on over the nut. An adjustable spanner is handy when the right size is not available, but it is the most likely to slip, so it is set tight and pulled with the load on the fixed jaw. A 6-point socket grips the flats of the nut, so it is best on tight or rusted nuts. A 12-point socket is easier to fit in tight spaces because it fits in more positions, but it is more likely to round off a tight nut. A torque wrench is used last, to tighten bolts to the torque given in the specification, and never to undo nuts. For most work I would use the right-sized ring spanner or 6-point socket, then the torque wrench for final tightening.
markingPoints: Open-ended: quick and fits from the side, but can slip
Ring spanner: grips all corners, best for breaking tight nuts
Adjustable: handy but slips; set tight, load on the fixed jaw
6-point grips better than 12-point; 12-point fits in more positions
Torque wrench only for final tightening to a specified torque, never for undoing

essays.stem: Explain the extra precautions needed when using hand tools in these places: near flammable vapour, near electrical equipment, and on a raised platform.
essays.modelAnswer: Near flammable vapour, such as beside a fuel tank, a spark from a steel tool striking steel could start a fire or explosion. The work needs a permit and a gas test first, and non-sparking tools made of copper alloys are usually chosen. These tools reduce the risk but do not remove it, so the permit, gas testing and ventilation are still needed. Near electrical equipment, the circuit must be isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead with a tester that is checked before and after use. Insulated tools are used as an extra protection, never as a reason to work live, and they are checked for damage to the insulation. On a raised platform or scaffold, a dropped tool can seriously injure someone below. Tools are tied on with lanyards or kept in a tool bag, the area below is barricaded, and toe boards are in place. In every case I would check the risk assessment, brief the team and follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: Flammable vapour: permit, gas test, non-sparking tools, which reduce but do not remove the risk
Electrical: isolate, lock off, tag, prove dead with a checked tester
Insulated tools are extra protection only, never for live work, and are checked
Height: lanyards or tool bags, barricade below, toe boards
Risk assessment, team briefing, maker's instructions and Centre rules

essays.stem: Your team will spend most of a week sawing, filing and tapping by hand. Explain how you would reduce the risk of strain injuries to their hands, wrists, arms and backs.
essays.modelAnswer: Hand tool work repeated for hours can cause strain injuries, such as pain and swelling in the wrists and forearms, and back pain from poor posture. To reduce this, I would first make sure the tools are sharp and in good order, because blunt files, saws and taps need much more force. I would choose tools with handles that fit the hand and do not have sharp edges. I would set the vice at the right height, about elbow height, so each person can work with a straight back and a straight wrist, and use packing or a different bench for shorter or taller people. Work is clamped firmly so that people are not gripping it as well. I would rotate the tasks, so nobody saws or files all day, and plan short breaks with stretches. I would brief the team to report any pain early, and keep an eye on how they are working, correcting poor posture or grip as I see it.
markingPoints: Names strain injuries and their causes
Sharp, well-kept tools with handles that fit the hand
Vice or bench at the right height; straight wrist and back; work clamped
Task rotation and short breaks
Team told to report pain early; leader watches and corrects posture

essays.stem: Explain how you would choose the hacksaw blade and method for cutting each of these: thin-walled square tube, 50 × 50 × 5 mm angle, and a solid 30 mm round bar.
essays.modelAnswer: The main rule is that at least three teeth should be in the cut at all times, so the finer the section, the finer the blade. For thin-walled square tube, I would use a fine blade, about 32 TPI, and start the cut on a corner at a low angle, then turn the tube so I am always cutting through the wall at a slant, not straight down onto a thin edge. For the 50 × 50 × 5 mm angle, a 24 TPI blade suits the 5 mm thickness. I would start on the outside edge of one leg and saw at an angle, turning the work in the vice so I never cut along the full width of a thin leg at once. For the solid 30 mm bar, a coarser blade, about 18 TPI, cuts faster and clears the chips. I would make a small nick to start, then use long, steady strokes with pressure on the forward stroke only. In each case the work is clamped close to the cut, the blade is tight with teeth facing forward, and I slow down at the end so the piece does not drop.
markingPoints: States the rule of at least three teeth in the cut
Thin tube: fine blade (about 32 TPI) and cutting at a slant through the wall
Angle: about 24 TPI, start on an edge, turn the work to avoid long thin cuts
Solid bar: coarser blade (about 18 TPI), long steady strokes
Work clamped close to the cut, blade tensioned, slow at the end of the cut

essays.stem: Describe the hand tools used to prepare joints before welding and to clean welds afterwards, and explain how to avoid contaminating stainless steel and aluminium.
essays.modelAnswer: Before welding, files are used to remove burrs and sharp edges and to dress the bevel and root face, and a scraper or file removes paint and scale near the joint. Wire brushes clean off rust and dirt, and clamps hold the parts in line for tacking. After welding, a chipping hammer removes the slag, used with safety glasses because slag chips fly, and a wire brush cleans the weld between passes and at the end. A cold chisel or file can remove spatter. For stainless steel and aluminium, the tools must be kept for that metal only and marked, for example with coloured tape. A brush with carbon steel bristles, or a file used on carbon steel, leaves tiny bits of iron in the surface, which rust and spoil stainless steel and can cause defects in aluminium welds. So stainless steel is cleaned with stainless steel brushes, and aluminium with its own stainless brushes and clean files. The tools are stored apart from the carbon steel tools, and the work is kept off carbon steel benches.
markingPoints: Preparation tools: files, scrapers, wire brushes, clamps, with their uses
Cleaning tools: chipping hammer, wire brush, chisel or file for spatter
Eye protection when chipping slag
Explains contamination: iron from carbon steel tools causes rust or defects
Separate, marked tools for stainless and aluminium, stored apart

essays.stem: A specification says the flange bolts must be tightened to 80 N·m. Explain why bolts are tightened to a set torque, how to use a click-type torque wrench correctly, and how to look after it. Include how 80 N·m relates to the force on a 400 mm handle.
essays.modelAnswer: Bolts are tightened to a set torque so that they clamp the joint with the right force. Too little and the joint can leak or work loose; too much and the bolt can stretch, the thread can strip or a gasket can be crushed. Torque is force times distance, so on a 400 mm handle, 80 N·m needs a force of 80 ÷ 0.4 = 200 N at the hand grip. To use the wrench, I check its calibration label, set it to 80 N·m and lock the setting. I first run the nuts down by hand with a spanner, then tighten them in a crossing (star) pattern in two or three stages, so the flange pulls down evenly. I pull smoothly on the handle grip, at right angles to the wrench, and stop as soon as it clicks, never pulling on past the click. Afterwards, I wind the setting back to its lowest value, wipe it clean and store it in its case. I never use it to undo nuts or as a hammer, and if it is dropped I send it for checking.
markingPoints: Explains why torque matters: right clamping force, no loosening, stretching or stripping
Correct calculation: 80 ÷ 0.4 = 200 N
Checks calibration, sets and locks the value
Tightens in a star pattern in stages, smooth pull, stops at the click
Care: wound back to lowest setting, cleaned, cased, not used to undo, checked if dropped

practical1.title: Plan, make and inspect a bolted bracket assembly using hand tools
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the team a drawing of a bolted bracket assembly: a base plate and an angle cleat in 6 mm mild steel, joined by two M10 bolts into tapped holes, with a filed radius on one corner and a threaded rod stud. As a team, write a short plan: the steps, the hand tools for each step, the quality checks and who does what. Each member then makes at least one part, or one set of features, using only hand tools: marking out, hacksawing, filing to size and to the radius, deburring, tapping the M10 holes (the tapping holes are drilled on the pillar drill by the assessor or under the assessor's direct supervision), and threading the stud with a die. Every member must cut, file and tap or thread at least once. The team checks each part against the drawing and records the sizes, then assembles the bracket and tightens the bolts with a torque wrench to the value the assessor gives. Finally, clean, check and return all the tools. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and the plan to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the assembly and the check sheet are finished.
materials: Mild steel plate and angle (6 mm) and 10 mm round bar, cut roughly to size
Scriber, engineer's square, steel rule, centre punch and ball pein hammer
Hacksaws with 18 and 24 TPI blades, flat, half-round and smooth files, file card
M10 tap set, tap wrench, M10 die and die stock, cutting fluid
M10 bolts and washers, ring spanners and a click-type torque wrench
Bench vices with soft jaws, clamps, a vernier caliper and radius gauges
A planning sheet and a check sheet
photos: The team's plan, with tools and tasks listed
Parts marked out, with the lines and punch marks clear
Members sawing and filing, with work clamped correctly
A hole being tapped, with the tap started square
The finished parts laid out with the check sheet
The bracket assembled, with the torque wrench on a bolt
The tools cleaned and back on the shadow board or in the kit
checklist: Took part in the plan and chose suitable tools for their tasks
Checked tools before use and reported any that were faulty
Sawed and filed accurately to the marked lines, with work clamped correctly
Tapped or threaded correctly: square start, cutting fluid, chips broken and cleared
Checked their parts against the drawing and recorded the sizes
Used the torque wrench correctly and set it back to its lowest setting
Worked safely and cleaned, checked and returned the tools
safety: Wear safety glasses and safety boots; wear gloves when handling sharp-edged steel, but not when using the pillar drill
Clamp all work firmly before sawing, filing or tapping
Use only tools in good condition, with handles fitted to all files
Deburr sharp edges and keep fingers clear of the saw blade
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Inspect and recondition a hand tool kit, and set up a tool control system
practical2.brief: The assessor provides a mixed kit of the Centre's hand tools, including some with faults (for example a mushroomed chisel, a blunt cold chisel, a rounded screwdriver, a loose hammer handle, a spanner with spread jaws and a clogged file). As a team, inspect every tool against a checklist and sort them into 'fit for use', 'repair' and 'scrap'. Each member reconditions at least two tools, for example dressing a chisel or punch head, regrinding a cold chisel or screwdriver tip (on the bench grinder only under the assessor's direct supervision), cleaning a file with a file card, or fitting and wedging a new hammer handle. Tools that cannot be repaired safely are tagged and recorded for scrapping. Then set up a tool control system for the kit: a numbered register, a shadow board or labelled layout, a sign-out sheet and an inspection tag or colour for this month. Finally, the team gives a 10-minute toolbox talk to the class on the safe use and care of hand tools, and every member speaks. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and the register to the group's practical.
materials: A mixed kit of hand tools, some with faults, chosen by the assessor
Tool inspection checklist and register sheets
'Do not use' tags, inspection tags or coloured tape, and marker pens
A board, outline paint or tape for a shadow board
Bench grinder (assessor supervised), files, file card, new hammer handle and wedges
Flip chart or paper for the toolbox talk
photos: The kit sorted into fit for use, repair and scrap, with the checklist
Each faulty tool before repair, showing the fault
A member reconditioning a tool, wearing the right PPE
The register, sign-out sheet and the shadow board with tools in place
The team giving the toolbox talk
checklist: Inspected tools in a set order and found the faults correctly
Sorted tools correctly into fit for use, repair and scrap
Reconditioned tools safely and to a usable standard
Kept a chisel or screwdriver cool when grinding, and wore a face shield
Tagged and recorded unsafe tools clearly
Filled in the register and sign-out sheet clearly and helped set up the shadow board
Spoke clearly in the toolbox talk on the safe use and care of hand tools
safety: Use the bench grinder only under the assessor's direct supervision, with guards and tool rest set and a face shield worn
Hold tools being reconditioned firmly; clamp them where possible
Wear safety glasses at all times, and gloves when handling sharp or rusty tools
Do not use any tool tagged 'Do not use'
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
